finding: The live range of $220-$775 is about right. Built totals for the front axle (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Mazda3 2.0L about $191-$605 (0.6-1.5 hr); midsize 2012 Dodge Grand Caravan about $196-$564 (0.6-1.3 hr); truck 2016 F-150 about $353-$710 (1.0-1.5 hr); luxury 2015 Acura RDX about $244-$555 (0.7-0.9 hr). The live floor of $220 sits a little above our lowest totals ($191-$196), and those pair low-priced aftermarket parts bought online with a manufacturer warranty time, both less than a shop normally charges; AAA and KBB start at $250. The live top of $775 covers our highest total (truck with list-price Ford parts, about $710) with a little room. A European luxury car at a dealer, with genuine parts, wear sensors and a higher labor rate, can plausibly exceed $775; that case is not priced here. How solid the labor times are: every low end is a stated time for the example vehicle itself. Three are manufacturer warranty times for exactly this job: Mazda's 0.6 hr to replace front pads and both discs on a 2014-2016 Mazda3, Chrysler's 0.6 hr to replace front pads and rotors on a 2011-2012 Grand Caravan, and Acura's 0.7 hr (discs plus pads, printed the same way in two separate bulletins) on a 2013-2015 RDX. The truck low end is a parts seller's 1-hour install estimate for the F-150, repeated on three of its front kits; the same seller prints 2 hours on a 2018-2020 kit and 3 hours on another 2010-2020 kit, so its figures are loose. The high ends are now mixed. Midsize and luxury use the maker's own longer line for the same axle: Chrysler's 1.3 hr and Acura's 0.9 hr to replace the pads and resurface (refinish) the discs instead of replacing them. Those are for the example vehicle, but they are still warranty times, the bottom of what shops bill, so the tops of those two classes ($564 and $555) are more likely to be too low than too high; with the 1.5 hr used before they would be about $596 and $651. The economy high end, 1.5 hr, is the lower figure of Haynes's 1h30-2h30 estimate on its Mazda 3 page, which is for the model but covers every generation with one figure and reads as templated; at Haynes's 2.5 hr the economy top would be about $765. The truck high end is unchanged and is still not for a truck: a technician-run advice site's 1.5 hr (1.0 for pads plus 0.5 for rotors) on a 2019 Honda Odyssey, supported loosely by The Drive's 'an hour per axle'. No trade-press book time was found for any of the four vehicles (the Brake & Front End Mazda3 brake job article covers 2004-2013 and states no time). Seized hardware, rust or caliper work will push real jobs past these times. Confidence is raised to medium because every class has a stated time and two parts sources and seven of the eight hours figures are now for the example model, but four of those seven are warranty times and one is a templated publisher estimate, so treat the high totals as soft. Not found: a manufacturer time for front pads and rotors alone on a full-size pickup (GM bulletin 22-NA-165 prints 2.1 hr for front and rear pads and rotors together on a 2023-2025 Silverado 1500, which cannot be split by axle; Ford, Toyota and BMW bulletins print none). The midsize example is a minivan from 2012 because that is the vehicle whose maker prints the time. Our totals sit below RepairPal's $574-$698; the gap is mostly parts (our low ends are online aftermarket prices of $119-$233, RepairPal's parts figure is $406-$452). No change to the live range is supported by this evidence. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): the midsize and luxury high ends were put back to 1.5 hr. The 1.3 hr Chrysler and 0.9 hr Acura lines pay for pads plus rotor resurfacing, not new rotors, and are warranty times, so they are kept as cross-checks only. Built totals at $120-$160/hr: midsize $196-$596, luxury $244-$651. The economy 1.5 hr now also appears in a Haynes guide for the Mazda3 (1.5-2.5 hr, a home-mechanic figure on a templated page). Confidence stays low: no class has a shop-level upper time for its own vehicle.
extras: Quotes often add: brake hardware/clip kit and pad-wear sensors (European cars), brake fluid flush, caliper service or replacement if seized or leaking, rotor machining instead of replacement, shop supplies and disposal fees, inspection or diagnosis fee, and sales tax. The rear axle is priced separately.
